summary: Question: can cash and commodity futures yield curves be modelled and forecast? Method: decompose each curve into unconditional, mean-reverting maturity-specific and contract-rolling date-specific components with exponential bases, fitted to cleaned CRB futures data. Conclusion: out-of-sample curve forecasts beat a random walk for heating oil, natural gas, soybeans and long-horizon crude; data should be handled contract by contract.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Interest rates earned on treasury bills/bonds of different maturity (7 Nov 08).
claims.claim: The cash yield curve is the set of Treasury rates across maturities on one day; on 7 Nov 2008 it was steeply upward sloping from near zero at 3 months to over 4% at 30 years.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Interest rates derived from contracts in the Eurodollar option market.
claims.claim: The authors' cash curve is built from Eurodollar (3-month LIBOR) futures/option contracts and expressed as instantaneous forward rates, giving many more maturity points than the Treasury curve.
claims.exact_rule: Cash curve = instantaneous forward rates implied by Eurodollar contract prices at each listed expiry (out to ~10 years)
claims.data_needed: Eurodollar futures prices for all listed expiries
claims.indicator: Eurodollar 3-month LIBOR contracts, instantaneous forward rates
claims.testable: partly - slide deck gives no full specification

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Plot shows instantaneous forward rates.
claims.claim: In early 2008 (2008.16) the Eurodollar forward curve dipped from about 3.1% at the front to about 2.6-2.7% near one year and then rose steadily to about 5.8% at 10 years.
claims.reported_result: Chart 2008.16: ~3.1% at tau~0.2, trough ~2.6-2.7% near tau~0.7-1, ~4.3% at 4y, ~5.0% at 6y, ~5.8% at 10y (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Interest rates implied by the prices of contracts for delivery of a commodity at some future date.
claims.claim: A commodity 'yield curve' is the continuously compounded rate implied by the slope of the futures price curve across delivery dates, so it mixes interest, storage and convenience effects.
claims.exact_rule: Commodity yield at maturity tau = d log F_t(tau) / d tau (see C20 for discrete version)
claims.data_needed: daily settlement prices of all listed futures contracts (CRB Trader), by contract expiry
claims.testable: partly - slide deck gives no full specification

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Light crude oil, same date as prior slide
claims.claim: On the same early-2008 date the light crude implied yield was negative at the short end (about -0.03 %/unit) rising through zero near 2.5 years to about +0.01 at 8.5 years, i.e. backwardated front and contango back.
claims.reported_result: Chart 2008.16: ~-0.03 at tau<0.5, ~0 at tau~2.5, ~+0.005 at tau 4-5, ~+0.01 at tau~8.5 (read from image; axis labelled %)
claims.indicator: WTI light crude futures implied yield curve

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Can you predict where it’s headed?
claims.claim: The research question is how the yield curves of cash and commodities move over time, whether their future shape can be predicted, and how commodity curves (which embed convenience) relate to the cash curve and to each other.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Some changes are large, other curves cluster together
claims.claim: Over about 100 days, cash yield curves sampled 10 trading days apart showed occasional large shifts (mostly at the short end) while other periods barely moved.
claims.reported_result: Chart: short end moved from ~3% (red, original) to ~4.5-5.5% across curves; 10y end clustered ~5.7-6.1% (read from image)
claims.conditions: change is uneven: large jumps at front end, little at long end

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Rather different appearance from cash, with much less smoothness
claims.claim: Crude oil implied yield curves over the same 100 days are far less smooth than cash curves and move most at the short end.
claims.reported_result: Chart: short-end yields range ~-0.02 to ~-0.10 across curves 10 days apart; long end near 0 to +0.01 (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Dependent movements over 10-day intervals for heating oil and light crude.
claims.claim: Heating oil and light crude implied yield curves move together over 10-day intervals, so curves of related products are linked.
claims.data_needed: CL and HO futures prices (CRB Trader)
claims.reported_result: Chart over tau 0.2-1.35 years: CL curves ~-0.15 to ~0 rising with tau; HO curves +0.2 to -0.2 (read from image)
claims.indicator: HO and CL implied yield curves
claims.testable: yes - joint dynamics of two curves

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Strong seasonal pattern for heating oil that is not apparent in yield on light crude.
claims.claim: Heating oil's implied yield curve has a strong seasonal shape across delivery months (positive then negative over about a year), which crude does not show, so any curve model must allow product-specific seasonality.
claims.reported_result: Chart: HO yields ~+0.2 at tau 0.4-0.7, cross zero ~0.8, trough ~-0.2 near tau 0.9-1.0, back positive ~1.2 (read from image)
claims.indicator: heating oil implied yield by delivery month
claims.direction: HO yield positive into winter delivery, negative after
claims.testable: yes - seasonal dummies by delivery month

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Rather than have to predict a “curve”, forecast the value of certain parameters in a regression- like formula for the curve
claims.claim: Parametric models make curve forecasting tractable because one forecasts a few state parameters instead of every maturity point.
claims.exact_rule: Forecast the time series of model coefficients, then rebuild the curve from them
claims.testable: yes - compare parameter forecasts with random walk

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Model used resembles a polynomial, but on a logarithmic scale more suited to description of rates.
claims.claim: The curve model is polynomial-like in exponential (log-scale) terms of maturity, which the authors view as a better description of rates than plain polynomials.
claims.exact_rule: Basis functions are sums of exponentials e^{-j k tau} (polynomial in e^{-k tau})
claims.testable: partly - slide deck gives no full specification

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Does the model allow arbitrage?
claims.claim: Key unresolved modelling choices are how many polynomial terms to use and whether the fitted model admits arbitrage; details are deferred to the paper.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Decompose the yield curve y t (τ) into three components
claims.claim: Each yield curve y_t(tau) is split into a long-run unconditional curve U(tau), a maturity-specific component M_t(tau) and a date-specific component D_t(tau).
claims.exact_rule: y_t(tau) = U(tau) + M_t(tau) + D_t(tau); E_s y_s(tau) = U(tau)
claims.data_needed: daily settlement prices of all listed futures contracts (CRB Trader), by contract expiry
claims.testable: partly - slide deck gives no full specification

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Maturity specific component is mean reverting
claims.claim: The maturity-specific part factors as M_t(tau) = m_t g(tau), with m_t a mean-reverting lognormal process whose expectation decays as m_s e^{-k(t-s)}, so its shape at a fixed maturity fades back toward the unconditional curve.
claims.exact_rule: M_t(tau) = m_t g(tau); m_t follows lognormal SDE with E_s m_t = m_s exp(-k (t-s)), s<t
claims.testable: yes - estimate k and test decay of m_t

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Date specific term is also mean reverting, but captures effects that move toward origin with time
claims.claim: The date-specific component is attached to a delivery date: a shock to a contract rolls down the curve toward maturity zero as time passes, E_s D_t(tau) = D_s(tau+t-s), so each contract carries its own effect.
claims.exact_rule: E_s D_t(tau) = D_s(tau + t - s) for s<t
claims.testable: yes - test whether contract-level deviations persist to expiry

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: If d t follows log normal SDE, then h(τ) = e -kτ
claims.claim: If the date-specific state d_t follows a lognormal mean-reverting SDE, the date component has basis h(tau) = e^{-k tau} and E_s D_t(tau) = (d_s e^{-k(t-s)}) e^{-k tau}.
claims.exact_rule: D_t(tau) = d_t e^{-k tau}; E_s D_t(tau) = d_s e^{-k(t-s)} e^{-k tau} = D_s(tau+t-s)
claims.testable: partly - slide deck gives no full specification

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: 2 maturity-specific functions
claims.claim: Their example specification (2,2,3) uses a 2nd-order unconditional curve, two maturity-specific functions c(e^{-k tau} - e^{-2k tau}) and c(e^{-k tau} - e^{-4k tau}), and three date-specific functions.
claims.exact_rule: Model (2,2,3): U = 2nd-order; m_{t,1} = c_m1 (e^{-k tau} - e^{-2 k tau}); m_{t,2} = c_m2 (e^{-k tau} - e^{-4 k tau}); 3 date-specific exponential functions
claims.testable: yes - specification is given except k and the 3 date functions

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Constant k determines shapes
claims.claim: The maturity components are humps that start at zero, peak within the first half-year and vanish by about 2 years, while date components are decaying exponentials from 1; the decay constant k sets their shapes.
claims.reported_result: Chart M_t(tau): humps peaking ~0.25-0.38 at tau~0.15-0.35, ~0 by tau 2; D_t(tau): exponentials from 1.0 decaying to ~0-0.05 by tau 3 (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Estimates are smoother than those for each day
claims.claim: State coefficients extracted jointly over several days give smoother fitted curves than fitting each day separately; the fit splits the curve into unconditional, maturity and date parts.
claims.reported_result: Chart 2006.87: observed yields ~0.5 at front decaying to ~0 by tau 2 and ~-0.02 beyond; date component (blue) dominates front, maturity component (green) trough ~-0.19 near tau 0.15, unconditional (red) ~-0.07 rising to ~0 (read from image)
claims.testable: partly - slide deck gives no full specification

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Observation error ought to be uncorrelated
claims.claim: The specification check is that residual observation errors should be uncorrelated across maturities once the three components are fitted.
claims.exact_rule: Diagnostic: residuals of fitted curve should be serially/cross-sectionally uncorrelated

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Recursively update as forecast extends beyond initial training period
claims.claim: Forecasts extrapolate the fitted state model and are re-estimated recursively as the out-of-sample period extends past the initial training window.
claims.exact_rule: Expanding-window re-estimation; forecast state coefficients h days ahead (65, 125, 250) and rebuild curve
claims.data_needed: daily settlement prices of all listed futures contracts (CRB Trader), by contract expiry
claims.testable: partly - slide deck gives no full specification

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Negative values indicate our models dominate random walk (Newey-West statistic)
claims.claim: Out of sample, the model forecasts of commodity yield curves beat a random-walk (no-change) curve forecast in almost all cases, most strongly for heating oil and soybeans; the one exception is crude at 65 days.
claims.reported_result: Newey-West statistic (negative = model beats random walk): Crude 65d 2.1, 125d -0.09, 250d -2.2; Heating oil -5.8, -8.7, -2.2; Natural gas -1.6, -2.2, -1.4; Soybean -5.1, -7.4, -3.1
claims.indicator: forecast-loss comparison vs random walk (Newey-West statistic)
claims.direction: model curve forecast better than no-change forecast
claims.conditions: crude at 65 days is worse than random walk (+2.1) and about equal at 125 days
claims.testable: yes - Diebold-Mariano style test with Newey-West errors

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Never underestimate the time that it takes to prepare the data.
claims.claim: Data preparation for futures curves is the main practical burden of the project.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Obtain prices of futures contracts from data vendor CRB Trader
claims.claim: Yields are not observed directly; they are derived from futures contract prices obtained from the vendor CRB Trader.
claims.data_needed: daily settlement prices of all listed futures contracts (CRB Trader), by contract expiry

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Prices are much smoother
claims.claim: Futures price curves are much smoother than the implied yield curves derived from them, which motivates working with prices.
claims.reported_result: Chart 2008.16 crude: price curve smooth U-shape from ~$91 at front to ~$87 at tau~3 then ~$90.4 at tau~9; implied yield step-like and noisy (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Compute the yield at the midpoint between two observed prices as the continuously compounded rate of interest
claims.claim: The implied yield at the midpoint between two adjacent contracts is the log-price difference divided by the maturity gap (continuous compounding).
claims.exact_rule: y_t(tau + d/2) = [log p_t(tau+d) - log p_t(tau)] / d for adjacent expiries tau and tau+d (limit d->0)
claims.data_needed: daily settlement prices of all listed futures contracts (CRB Trader), by contract expiry

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Differencing magnifies random noise
claims.claim: Deriving yields by differencing prices magnifies noise; yields exist only at discrete points, the terminal date is about 15 days, there is no observed spot rate, and microstructure anomalies appear.
claims.reported_result: terminal date about 15 days (shortest usable maturity)
claims.conditions: worst at short maturities and around illiquid contracts

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Ripple induced by preference for contract at a specific date (market microstructure)
claims.claim: Cash (LIBOR) yield curves about 10 days apart show a ripple caused by traders' preference for specific contract dates, a microstructure artefact rather than economic information.
claims.reported_result: Chart 1995.28: three LIBOR curves ~7.0-8.6%, with saw-tooth ripples along maturity (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: A contract for light crude did not trade this day, so price stayed same as on prior day
claims.claim: When one crude contract does not trade its stale price creates a spurious spike in the implied yield curve while the rest of the curve has moved.
claims.reported_result: Chart 1999.35: implied yield spikes to ~-0.14 then ~+0.05 near tau 2.2-2.4 around a stale price (~$16.0 vs curve) (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Approach is to follow a contract over time rather than fixed maturity
claims.claim: Anomalies are patched with an adaptive procedure applied along each contract's own time series (fixed expiry date t+tau) rather than along fixed maturities, avoiding interpolation artefacts.
claims.exact_rule: Clean y_t(tau) along diagonals with fixed expiry date t+tau (contract series), not along constant-maturity series

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Contracts have a more consistent sequential pattern than in yields over varying maturities
claims.claim: A single contract's yield evolves more consistently over time than constant-maturity yields, which is why cleaning by contract works better.
claims.testable: yes - compare autocorrelation of contract vs constant-maturity series

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Outliers are more easily identified in the sequence of yields associated with contract rather than over the yield curve itself.
claims.claim: Outliers stand out as isolated jumps in a contract's yield history, whereas on a single day's curve they are hard to tell from real kinks.
claims.reported_result: Chart: one contract's yield over days ~35100-35900 with isolated spikes (~-0.16, ~+0.27) against a smooth path peaking ~0.3 near day 35750 (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: In order not to distort “real” prices, miss a few outliers.
claims.claim: The cleaning filter is deliberately conservative: it leaves some outliers in place to avoid altering genuine prices.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Moving medians of length 3 cannot patch a period with a sustained anomaly.
claims.claim: The patching filter is a running median of length 3 along each contract, which removes isolated spikes but cannot fix anomalies that last several days.
claims.exact_rule: Replace each contract-yield observation by the median of itself and its neighbours (window 3)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: persists for about 3 weeks
claims.claim: One anomaly in the data persisted for about 3 weeks, so a short median filter leaves it in.
claims.reported_result: Chart: contract yield drops to ~-1.2 to -1.6 around day 35700 for about 3 weeks; cross-section shows discontinuity near tau~2.1 (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Cannot hold maturity τ fixed unless were able to observe y t (τ) for all t
claims.claim: Standard time-series methods need constant-maturity series, which are not observed; interpolating creates artefacts.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Following a single contract provides most direct series
claims.claim: Modelling each contract's own yield path gives the most direct observed time series, versus a structural curve model f(tau) that can be evaluated at any maturity.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Contracts end, becoming more variable as τ approaches 0 where yield is more volatile.
claims.claim: Contract yields become much more volatile as they approach expiry.
claims.reported_result: Chart (Day 35694): contract rates up to ~0.45 within ~100 rows of expiry, near 0 (±0.05) beyond ~200 rows (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Very strong presence of outliers as τ nears 0
claims.claim: The standard deviation of contract yields falls steeply with time to expiry, and near expiry it is dominated by outliers, so a robust scale estimate is much lower than the plain SD.
claims.reported_result: 'SD over Contracts': sd ~0.33 at 0 rows to expiry, ~0.17 at 50, ~0.08 at 200, ~0.04 at 400; robust fit ~0.21 at 0 converging to sd beyond ~50 rows (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Non−Gaussian variation near origin
claims.claim: Variation in contract yields near expiry is non-Gaussian, so Gaussian time-series methods are inappropriate at the front end.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Differences in yields of adjacent contracts are non-stationary as time gap increases
claims.claim: Yield differences between contracts become non-stationary as the gap between their expiries widens, suggesting contracts are cointegrated only when close together.
claims.exact_rule: Test stationarity of y_t(contract i) - y_t(contract j) as a function of expiry gap
claims.conditions: cointegration holds when contracts are not 'too far' apart

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Degree of time separation also measures the rate of change in the yield curve, a sort of stochastic modulus of continuity of the yield
claims.claim: How far apart contracts can be while staying cointegrated measures how quickly the yield curve changes shape.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Interpret the source of non-stationarity as due to movements of some underlying yield process
claims.claim: Non-stationarity is attributed to a latent underlying yield process common to the contracts, pointing to a latent-variable model.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Prices again seem simpler to use
claims.claim: Prices of four crude contracts about 100 days apart move almost identically in mid-1984, so contract prices share a common driver.
claims.reported_result: Chart mid 1984: four contracts ~$25-31 overlapping closely (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Plot shows prices of 4 contracts for light crude, about 100 days apart
claims.claim: In 2007-08 the same pattern holds: four crude contracts about 100 days apart track each other as prices rise from about $50 to $120.
claims.reported_result: Chart early 2007 onwards: prices ~$50 rising to ~$120 with the four contracts nearly overlapping (read from image)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: How to use the evident contemporaneous movements in prices or yields for various products (such as the various soy commodities)
claims.claim: Related products (e.g. soybean complex) move together contemporaneously and with the cash yield, so a multivariate model is a natural next step.
claims.indicator: soy complex futures curves and cash yield

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Model after subtracting out the yield for cash to extract a convenience yield
claims.claim: Subtracting the cash yield from a commodity's implied yield isolates its convenience yield, which might be stationary and simpler to model.
claims.exact_rule: Convenience-type yield = commodity implied yield y_t(tau) minus cash yield at same tau (proposed, not tested)
claims.data_needed: daily settlement prices of all listed futures contracts (CRB Trader), by contract expiry; Eurodollar curve

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Out-of-sample performance superior to random walk benchmark
claims.claim: The authors conclude that their decomposed yield-curve models capture curve dynamics and forecast better out of sample than a random walk.
claims.reported_result: see Slide 17 Newey-West table

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Date and maturity specific decomposition relevant for commodities as well
claims.claim: The date-plus-maturity decomposition built for interest rates also applies to commodity futures curves.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Many unresolved questions
claims.claim: Working with contracts rather than a maturity function is preferable because of outliers and statistical convenience, but many questions remain open.

reasoning.question: Can the term structure of cash rates and of commodity futures (their implied 'yield curves') be modelled parsimoniously enough to forecast where the curve is heading, and how should noisy futures data be handled? For an investor this bears on forecasting carry/roll yield and curve shape in commodity futures.

thesis.statement: Decomposing a yield curve into a stable unconditional curve, a mean-reverting maturity-specific component and a date-specific component that rolls with each contract gives forecasts of commodity futures curves that beat a random walk out of sample; data should be handled contract by contract because yields derived from prices are noisy near expiry.

foundations.premise: Deviations of the curve from its long-run shape mean-revert at a rate k.
foundations.support: assumed lognormal mean-reverting SDEs; no test shown

foundations.premise: Some shocks belong to a specific delivery date and travel with that contract toward expiry.
A commodity futures curve can be read as an implied interest-rate curve that includes convenience effects.
Futures prices are smoother and cleaner than the yields derived from them; contract time series are more consistent than constant-maturity series.
Related commodities share a common latent driver.
foundations.support: co-movement charts, cointegration of nearby contracts

mechanism_chain.why: log-price slope between adjacent contracts is a continuously compounded rate
decays toward zero at rate k (mean reversion)

mechanism_chain.to: same shock at shorter maturity later
mechanism_chain.why: the effect rolls down the curve with the contract
predictable decay and roll-down are captured

design_rationale.choice: Forecast a few state parameters instead of the whole curve
design_rationale.alternatives: predicting the curve point by point

design_rationale.reason_given: better suited to describing rates; implied by lognormal SDE
design_rationale.sensitivity: number of terms and arbitrage-freeness flagged as open

design_rationale.choice: Clean data along each contract with a running median of 3
design_rationale.reason_given: outliers easier to see by contract; avoid interpolation artefacts; avoid distorting real prices
design_rationale.sensitivity: misses a few outliers and sustained (3-week) anomalies

design_rationale.choice: Work with contracts/prices rather than a function of maturity

evidence_map.result: Model beats random walk in 11 of 12 commodity/horizon cells (Newey-West statistic down to -8.7)
evidence_map.tests: steps 3-5: mean reversion and roll-down are forecastable
evidence_map.rules_out: that curve shape is a pure random walk for HO, NG, soybeans at 65-250 days
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) gains come from seasonality (HO, NG, soy) any seasonal model would capture; loss function and sample periods are not stated; no trading P&L shown
evidence_map.strength: moderate - out-of-sample but sample, loss and exact test not specified on slides

evidence_map.result: Crude at 65 days is worse than random walk (+2.1)
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) crude curve has little seasonality, so the model's edge may be seasonal

evidence_map.result: Contract yields are far more volatile and non-Gaussian near expiry
evidence_map.does_not_rule_out: (reader) delivery/liquidity effects rather than economic information

evidence_map.result: Nearby contracts appear cointegrated; spreads non-stationary as gap grows

regimes.condition: near expiry (tau below a few weeks)
regimes.effect: yields noisy, outlier-dominated, non-Gaussian; terminal usable date ~15 days
curve has a strong seasonal shape that the model must include
model does not beat random walk
stale prices create spurious yield spikes

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Number of terms, the value of k and arbitrage-freeness are left to the paper
Sample periods, training window length and loss function behind the forecast table are not given
Forecast accuracy of yields is not translated into a tradeable strategy or P&L
Median filter misses some outliers and sustained anomalies remain in the data
Convenience-yield extraction (commodity minus cash yield) is proposed but not tested
Observation errors 'ought to be' uncorrelated: the check is stated as a requirement, no result shown

relations.why: the implied yield curve is the term structure of carry; forecasting its shape forecasts roll yield
(reader) exponential basis with level/hump components resembles Nelson-Siegel with an added contract-specific component
heating-oil seasonality is a dominant feature of its curve

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) The current futures curve shape, decomposed into maturity-specific (mean-reverting at rate k) and contract-specific (rolling to expiry) parts, predicts the curve shape 3-12 months ahead, through steps 3-4 of the chain; the edge is largest for seasonal products (heating oil, soybeans, natural gas). It would stop working if curve deviations follow a random walk (no mean reversion), if seasonality is already fully priced into a seasonal-adjusted benchmark, or if data noise near expiry dominates.
reader_inferences: (reader) Model gains may largely reflect seasonality: the weakest result is crude, the least seasonal of the four.
(reader) No transaction-cost or trading test is given, so economic value of the forecast is unknown.
(reader) The yield units on the commodity charts are labelled % but read like decimal per-year rates; magnitudes should be rechecked from data.
(reader) The decomposition resembles Nelson-Siegel with an extra contract-specific factor.
(reader) Using CRB Trader settlement prices with a median-3 filter is a reproducible cleaning step for any futures term-structure signal.
